metadata.title: The Last Roadless Forests
metadata.description: Forty-five million acres of national forest have stayed roadless for 25 years. A proposed rule would end that. Here is what is at stake, who wants it, and who does not.

chapters.title: Eleven days
chapters.narrative:
On August 20, 2026, the Forest Service published a proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule in full. Public comments close on September 21. If the rule is finalized, 44.7 million acres of national forest that have stayed roadless for a quarter century become eligible for new roads and logging.

This story shows where those forests are, what they do for the people downstream and the towns next door, and what the government's own analysis says the change would be worth. The numbers come from the proposed rule, the Forest Service's data warehouse, federal economic statistics, and peer-reviewed research. The sources are listed at the end.

chapters.title: What roadless looks like
chapters.narrative: Prince of Wales Island in the Tongass National Forest. Spruce, hemlock, and cedar that were already old when the United States bought Alaska. Some of these trees have been standing for more than 500 years. Nothing about this stand has been managed, because nothing about it needed to be.
chapters.alt: A dense old-growth stand of moss-covered spruce and hemlock on Prince of Wales Island, with fallen logs on a green forest floor.
chapters.caption: Old growth on Prince of Wales Island, Tongass National Forest. USDA Forest Service Alaska Region, public domain.

chapters.title: Flying the Tongass
chapters.narrative: The Tongass is the largest national forest in the country and the largest intact temperate rainforest left on Earth. Roughly 9.3 million of its 16.7 million acres are inventoried roadless areas, shown here in orange over USGS imagery. Scroll to move between three of them.

keyframes.caption: Southeast Alaska. Every orange outline is a roadless area the proposed rule would open.
Honker Divide, Prince of Wales Island. A 30-mile canoe route through unlogged spruce and hemlock, on an island where most of the old growth has already been cut.
Admiralty Island. Roughly 1,500 brown bears live here, and bears outnumber people.
The Juneau Icefield roadless area. At 1.16 million acres it is the largest single roadless area in the inventory.

chapters.title: The forest, from the people who live in it
chapters.narrative: The Southeast Alaska Conservation Council, a regional group based in Juneau, on what old growth in the Tongass means for salmon, deer, and the communities that depend on both.

chapters.title: Fifty-eight million acres, forty-five of them on the table
chapters.narrative:
The 2001 rule covered 58.5 million acres of inventoried roadless areas in 37 states and Puerto Rico. Idaho and Colorado later wrote their own roadless rules, and the proposal leaves those in place (green). Everything in orange, 44.7 million acres, is covered by the national rule the administration wants to rescind.

More than nine in ten of those acres are in ten Western states. Alaska alone holds 14.8 million.

chapters.title: Where the roadless acres are
chapters.narrative: The twelve states with the most inventoried roadless acres. Idaho and Colorado are shown for scale; their state rules are not part of this proposal. Alaska's total is the Tongass and the Chugach together.

chapters.title: What the rule actually does
chapters.narrative:
The administration calls the Roadless Rule a "one-size-fits-all" barrier that has kept tens of millions of acres off-limits to forest treatments. That is not what the rule says. It prohibits new roads and commercial logging, not active management. It expressly allows generally small-diameter trees to be cut to restore ecosystems and reduce uncharacteristic wildfire effects. Roads may be built when an imminent fire, flood, or other emergency threatens lives or property. Prescribed fire, hunting, fishing, grazing, trails, and use of existing roads continue.

Local Forest Service officials already manage these lands and make project-level decisions within those exceptions. Rescission would remove the national floor against new roads and commercial logging; forest plans could retain protections, but local officials could later change them. The rule itself was written after more than 600 public hearings and 1.6 million comments, the largest public response to a federal rule at the time. It has survived two decades of litigation. The Tongass was exempted in 2020 and restored in 2023, which is why its roadless areas still appear here.

chapters.title: What the roads were for
chapters.narrative: Maybeso Valley, Prince of Wales Island, 1957. A single spar tree left standing in a clearcut, rigged to haul logs to the road. Between 1954 and the 1990s, long-term contracts with two pulp mills cut most of the biggest, oldest stands on the island. The roads that made it possible are still there. So are the second-growth thickets that replaced the forest.
chapters.alt: A black and white photograph of a lone tall spruce used as a spar tree, standing above a clearcut hillside on Prince of Wales Island in 1957.
chapters.caption: Spar tree above a clearcut, Maybeso Valley, Prince of Wales Island, August 1957. USDA Forest Service, public domain.

chapters.title: Dark Divide, Washington
chapters.narrative:
Roadless areas are not only an Alaska story. The Dark Divide in the Gifford Pinchot National Forest is the largest unprotected roadless area in western Washington, a ridge system between Mount St. Helens and Mount Adams where some trees are more than 500 years old. It is two hours from Portland. The Boundary Trail runs its length.

The orange outline is the inventoried roadless area. Everything else on this hillside already has roads.

chapters.title: The view people drive for
chapters.narrative: Mount Adams from Juniper Ridge in the Dark Divide. Views like this are the product a lot of southwest Washington now sells: guiding, lodging, restaurants, gear, gas. They depend on the forest staying the way it is.
chapters.alt: Mount Adams rising above forested ridges, seen from a trail in the Dark Divide Roadless Area.
chapters.caption: Mount Adams from the Dark Divide. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

chapters.title: Tourism is the economy now
chapters.narrative:
Outdoor recreation was 2.4 percent of U.S. GDP in 2024, $697 billion, and 5.2 million jobs, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. National forests alone draw about 159 million visits a year.

In Southeast Alaska, where the Tongass timber fight has run longest, the visitor industry employed 8,589 people in 2024 and paid $367 million in wages. Timber employed 274. The region set a cruise-passenger record the same year.

chapters.title: What the government says it is worth
chapters.narrative:
The proposed rule includes USDA's own estimate. Even if every operable roadless acre were logged, which the agency calls unlikely, the timber industry would gain $4.6 to $10.6 million a year and the Treasury $5.2 to $11.4 million. USDA also estimates recreation losses of $6.1 million a year. New roads cost $80,000 to more than $2 million per mile, on top of a $6.9 billion backlog of road maintenance the agency already cannot fund.

For comparison, the Forest Service lost an average of $44 million a year selling Tongass timber between 1980 and 2019. The beneficiaries are not the public and not the Treasury. They are a handful of regional mills and contractors, and the mining and energy leaseholders the rule notes would gain new flexibility.

chapters.title: This will not make lumber cheaper
chapters.narrative:
National forests supply about 4 percent of U.S. timber. USDA says rescission might add 5 to 10 percent to that slice, and probably less. That is a rounding error in a market where Canada supplies roughly a quarter of the softwood lumber Americans use.

Lumber prices move with housing starts, mill capacity, and trade policy. The 2021 spike was a pandemic housing boom. The 2025 rise followed duties and tariffs on Canadian lumber that now add about 45 percent to the price of imports. The Forest Service has lost a fifth of its workforce since early 2025 and industry analysts say ramping up federal harvest would take years and thousands of workers who do not exist.

chapters.title: The fire claim, tested
chapters.narrative:
The administration says more than 40 percent of roadless areas have high or very high wildfire hazard and only 5 percent of those high-hazard acres have received fuel treatments since 2014. Those figures describe hazard and treatment history; they do not show that the Roadless Rule caused fires or that rescission would reduce them. The agency's proposal makes a narrower case: the rule limits road-dependent mechanical thinning and some fire-control tactics. But the existing rule already permits prescribed fire, small-diameter thinning to reduce uncharacteristic wildfire effects, and emergency roads where an imminent threat endangers lives or property.

The government's own analysis says new management opportunities would be "modest and localized." It also concedes that greater access can increase human-caused ignitions. A 2026 study of every national forest in the lower 48 found about four times as many fires start within 50 meters of a road as in roadless areas or wilderness. A separate Oregon State University study found fire rates in roadless areas are no different from roaded national forest land. Roadless forests are not the fire problem.
chapters.xLabel: Setting, national forests in the lower 48, 1992 to 2024

chapters.title: Who wants this
chapters.narrative:
When the Forest Service asked for comment in 2025, it received letters on behalf of more than 625,000 people and organizations. An independent sample found 99 percent opposed. The proposed rule admits that most of the tribal governments it consulted oppose it. Hunting and fishing groups, county commissions, and 55 members of Congress filed against it.

A December 2025 national poll found 72 percent of likely voters oppose repeal, including 71 percent of Republicans. Support comes from the timber industry association, the homebuilders' lobby, Alaska's senators and governor, and the national association of counties. Those are the constituencies the rule serves.

chapters.title: Twenty-five million people drink from these watersheds
chapters.narrative:
A July 2026 study in PLOS Water traced surface drinking water for about 25 million Americans to watersheds influenced by roadless areas: 9.5 million in California, 3.3 million in Colorado, and towns across the interior West. Roadless areas hold the most intact forest in the national forest system, store a disproportionate share of its carbon, and provide habitat for more than 300 threatened and endangered species, by the Forest Service's own count.

Roads change all of that. They bring sediment into streams, fragment habitat, and open the door to the logging the rule was written to stop.

chapters.title: Still standing
chapters.narrative: Old growth in the Mt. Hood National Forest, an hour from Portland. The Roadless Rule has kept places like this the way they are for 25 years without a single new road. It costs nothing to keep. It would cost the public money to undo.
chapters.alt: Sunlight filtering through moss-draped branches of old-growth Douglas fir and hemlock in the Mt. Hood National Forest.
chapters.caption: Old growth, Mt. Hood National Forest. USDA Forest Service Pacific Northwest Region, public domain.

chapters.title: What you can do before September 21
chapters.narrative:
The Forest Service is accepting public comments on docket FS-2025-0001 at regulations.gov. It may group similar submissions rather than answer each one individually. A useful comment explains how the proposal would affect a specific place or use and gives reasons or evidence the agency can address. Say which forest you visit, what you do there, what you think the proposal would change, and why.
